lesson.title: Grading the Reaction: Percent Yield
lesson.summary: Percent yield expresses actual yield as a percentage of theoretical yield, giving chemists a single standardized number for how efficiently a reaction and lab procedure actually performed.
lesson.body:
Percent yield answers the question that actual yield and theoretical yield can each only half answer on their own: how good was this result, really? A student who collects 24.8 g of product might feel great or feel disappointed depending entirely on how much product was possible in the first place, so percent yield puts every result on the same comparable scale by turning it into a percentage.

The formula is straightforward: percent yield equals actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100 percent. Both yields must be in the same units, almost always grams, before you divide.

Using the zinc chloride example built up over the last two chapters, the theoretical yield was calculated as 27.1 g of ZnCl2, and the actual yield collected on the balance was 24.8 g. Percent yield is 24.8 g divided by 27.1 g, which equals 0.915, and multiplying by 100 percent gives 91.5 percent. That means the reaction and the lab technique together captured about 91.5 percent of the product that was theoretically possible, with the remaining roughly 8.5 percent lost to some combination of incomplete reaction, side reactions, or physical losses during filtering and drying.

A percent yield in the 90s, like this one, is generally considered a strong result for a hands-on lab procedure. Lower values point toward real problems worth investigating: maybe the reaction did not run long enough, maybe some product stayed dissolved in the filtrate instead of precipitating out, or maybe transfers between containers were sloppy. In principle, percent yield can never exceed 100 percent, since you cannot collect more product than the limiting reagent could possibly form. If a calculated percent yield does come out above 100 percent in real data, that is a red flag, not a triumph, and it almost always means the collected solid was not pure. It may still be wet, or it may have trapped some other salt or unreacted starting material, inflating its measured mass beyond what pure product would weigh.

Percent yield closes out the mass-based side of stoichiometry, but the same core skill, converting between amounts of two different substances using a balanced equation, applies just as well when the reactants are dissolved in solution rather than measured out as solids. That is where solution stoichiometry picks up next.
